objective: Mobile health, wearables and remote patient monitoring for self-management, and how to judge an app's quality, privacy and safety
secondaryObjectives: Health literacy and informed decision making

sources.cite: HHS Office for Civil Rights, Health App Use Scenarios and HIPAA (February 2016)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: a business associate 'creates, receives, maintains or transmits protected health information (PHI) on behalf of a covered entity'; when a provider contracts with a developer for patient management services delivered through an app, the developer is a business associate; when a consumer downloads an app on her own initiative, it is not. The case's clinic contracts the app for its patients, so the vendor needs a business associate agreement.

sources.cite: US Blood Pressure Validated Device Listing (VDL), Frequently Asked Questions
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: the VDL lists BP devices 'validated for clinical accuracy', with active FDA clearance, independent testing under an internationally accepted protocol and suitable cuff sizes; sponsored by the AMA and run by NORC with an independent review committee; quotes the 2017 AHA/ACC guideline that 'the BP measurement device used has been validated with an internationally accepted protocol'.

sources.cite: AMIA Accreditation Committee, foundational domains for master's-level health informatics education (CAHIIM HI master's curriculum requirements PDF)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. F6 (Social and Behavioral Aspects of Health): graduates 'Identify theories or models that explain and modify patient or population behaviors'; the MSHI course places mobile health and remote monitoring for self-management in F6.
Riverbend Family Medicine, the vendor, its app and cuffs, counts, costs and days are invented teaching values. The case names no reading, drug or dose and gives no clinical instruction.

brief.situation: You are the clinical informatics lead at Riverbend Family Medicine (fictional), a group of clinics. Leadership wants home blood pressure monitoring for 400 patients with hypertension, launching on day 30, using a vendor's app and Bluetooth cuffs. Your job is to judge the app's quality, privacy and safety and recommend how to launch.
handover: The clinics are a covered entity; the vendor would run the app for the clinics' patients.
The program budget is 80 thousand dollars.
howItWorks: The clock runs in days: each task takes days. Choose it, then let it finish, which moves the calendar on.
The board shows the program's risks against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words, the budget committed and the docket.
When you close the review you write the record and explain your reasoning.

writeup.question: For leadership: how you judged the app, what had to be true before launch, and why.

parts.label: Privacy
parts.criteria: The clinics contract the app for their patients, so the vendor handles PHI on their behalf and needs a business associate agreement; the advertising kit's sharing is found by reading the policy and testing traffic, and removed.
parts.modelAnswer: BAA signed; advertising kit out of the clinics' build.

parts.label: Quality and safety
parts.criteria: Readings that drive care need a validated device (the bundled cuff was not listed) and an alert path someone watches, with after-hours instructions.
parts.modelAnswer: Listed cuff in three sizes; flagged readings to the nurse line.

parts.label: Self-management and access
parts.criteria: Usability tested with real patients (think-aloud) and a route for those without smartphones, so the program reaches the patients it is for; launch on conditions rather than as offered or not at all.
parts.modelAnswer: Eight-patient test; cellular hubs; launched on day 30 with all four conditions.

launched.headline: Good: judged, then launched
launched.body: The app was judged the way a clinical tool should be: privacy terms read and tested, the device checked against a validated listing, the alert path given an owner, and usability tested with the patients it is for. It launched on time, on conditions.

costly.headline: Safe, at a cost
costly.body: Nothing harmful reached patients, but the program was declined, delayed, or launched without every condition, a key stakeholder, or a way in for patients without smartphones.

leakedEnd.headline: Data shared with advertisers
leakedEnd.body: A vendor running an app for a covered entity's patients is a business associate. Read the policy, test the traffic, and get a BAA and a clean build before launch.

alertEnd.headline: An alert nobody saw
alertEnd.body: Monitoring creates a duty to look. Route flagged readings to people who are on duty, and tell patients what to do when no one is.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No review record was written before the case's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: An mHealth app chosen by the clinics for their patients is a clinical tool, judged on privacy, quality, safety and access. Privacy: the vendor would handle PHI on the clinics' behalf, so it needs a business associate agreement, and the advertising kit the policy and traffic test reveal must go. Quality: readings that drive care need a cuff validated for accuracy; the bundled one is not listed. Safety: flagged readings need a watched path and after-hours instructions. Access and self-management: test with real patients and give those without smartphones a way in. Launch on those conditions.
